M1a.s: A list of numbers = an arrow in space example
M1a.t:
Keep just 2 numbers of 色’s vector, [3, 2], and it becomes an arrow on a plane: from the origin, 3 across and 2 up.
This site’s demo uses 16 numbers and large models use thousands; you cannot draw that, but the idea is the same: n numbers = an arrow in n-dimensional space.
Used in: layer 4 ③ embedding lookup
i: Turns a char into numbers you can compute with
Each number = how far along one direction
Look up the row by the char’s number
With numbers you can compare, add and transform

M1b.s: Chars with close meanings have close arrows example
M1b.t:
The cosine (cos) of the angle measures how close two directions are; 1 means the same direction:
蓝–绿 0.96 蓝–红 0.97 天–空 0.91
蓝–空 −0.32 (far apart)
Nobody places these arrows; training learns them: chars that appear in similar sentences slowly drift together.
i: Shows closeness of meaning as closeness of direction
One arrow per char; similar chars cluster
Training keeps moving the arrows
Similar chars share patterns: learn one, learn the group

c: ① How aligned two arrows are
M2a.s: How well two arrows line up, as one number example
M2a.t:
Dot product = length of q × length of k × cosθ (also = length of q × the green shadow):
3.16 × 3.20 × 0.84 ≈ 8.5
The more aligned and the longer the arrows, the bigger the dot product. In attention: the better 色’s question q lines up with 颜’s label k, the more 色 attends to 颜.
i: One number for how aligned two vectors are
Lengths and the angle (cosθ)
Multiply the lengths, then by the cosine
Aligned = related: a natural score

M2b.s: How: multiply matching positions, then add them all example
M2b.t:
Formula: q·k = q₁k₁ + q₂k₂ + … + qdkd
Only multiplying and adding, no angles; and the previous page’s “length × length × cosθ” gives exactly the same.
With d = 16 that is 16 multiplications + 15 additions.
i: Turns “how aligned” into simple arithmetic
d multiplications, then a sum
Multiply position by position, then sum
Just multiply-add: ideal for GPUs in bulk

M2c.s: Bigger = more similar; at right angles it is 0 example
M2c.t:
same way: big positive → closely related; right angle: 0 → unrelated; opposite: negative → opposite.
Dot product ÷ both lengths = cosine similarity (−1 to 1).
Attention does this once per pair of chars, giving the score table in layer 4.
i: Tells related, unrelated or opposite
Three outcomes: positive, 0, negative
Same way +, right angle 0, opposite −
Matches “how much to attend” as a score

M2d.s: Why divide by √d example
M2d.t:
Without it, scores are too big: softmax gives almost 100% to one char (98.17%), the others’ gradients are near 0, and learning stalls.
Divide by √d: scores return to a normal size and the percentages spread out, so training is stable. That is how the original paper explains it.
i: Brings attention scores back to a normal size
Dot product, dimension d, square root
Dot product ÷ √d, then softmax
Adding d terms gives variance d; ÷√d brings it back to 1

c: ① Vectors stack into a table
M3a.s:
Stack a row of vectors and you have a matrix example

天[0.2, −0.5, 0.7]
空[0.1, 0.3, −0.4]
色[−0.6, 0.8, 0.2]
3 chars, 3 numbers each

空0.10.3−0.4
色−0.60.80.2
X: 3 rows × 3 columns
Each row is one char’s vector; each column holds one dimension.
Numbers from the layer 4 ③ embedding-lookup example.
M3a.t:
A matrix is numbers laid out as a table; its size is written “rows × columns”.
In this site’s demo: 7 chars × 16 dims = a 7×16 matrix; the model’s parameters (like W_Q) are matrices too.
Why: all the chars together, computed in one go.
i: Puts the vectors of every char in a sentence together
Rows = chars, columns = dimensions
The whole table goes into the next step at once
Computing in bulk is far faster than one by one

i: Turns each char’s vector into Q, K, V
Rows of the left matrix, columns of the right
Dot a row with a column to fill one cell
One parameter table transforms every char at once

Two matrices Q and K; K is transposed
Q × Kᵀ: each cell is a dot product
GPUs are built for matrix multiplication: very fast

M4a.s:
Raw scores from the linear layer example

Which char comes after 色? Every char in the dictionary gets a score (4 drawn).
M4a.t:
Raw scores (logits) can be positive or negative, and do not add up to 1:
2.0 + 1.0 + 0.1 + (−0.5) = 2.6
They are not yet “how likely, in percent”. First make them positive, then share out 100% in proportion.
i: Gives every candidate char a score
Linear layer: vector × parameter matrix
Higher score = the model leans to that char
Scoring is simple, but not yet a probability

M4b.s:
Make them positive: take eˣ of each score example

e ≈ 2.718
eˣ is always above 0
bigger scores grow more
M4b.t:
e2.0 = 7.39 e1.0 = 2.72
e0.1 = 1.11 e−0.5 = 0.61
Negative scores turn positive too (−0.5 → 0.61), and the order stays: the highest is still the highest.
A score gap of 1 becomes a factor of e ≈ 2.7.
i: Turns scores of any sign into positive numbers
The exponential eˣ
Take eˣ of every score
Always positive, keeps the order, easy to differentiate

M4c.s:
Divide by the total to get percentages example

scoreeˣ÷ totalprob.
蓝2.07.397.39÷11.8262.5%
绿1.02.722.72÷11.8223.0%
红0.11.111.11÷11.829.3%
天−0.50.610.61÷11.825.1%
M4c.t:
Formula: softmax(xᵢ) = exᵢ ÷ (ex₁ + ex₂ + …)
The results all lie in 0–100% and add up to exactly 100%, so they work as probabilities. 蓝 is highest at 62.5%.
Layer 4’s [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] → [66%, 24%, 10%] is computed the same way.
i: Turns scores into probabilities that add to 100%
eˣ and the total
Each eˣ divided by the sum of all eˣ
Keeps order, differentiable; with cross-entropy the gradient is simple

M5a.s: How much the model gave the right answer example
M5a.t:
This is layer 4’s ④ error step: the parameters are still random, and 蓝 gets only 12%.
The other cells need no separate term: the more they take, the less 蓝 gets, and the error grows.
ln is the logarithm to base e; the next page draws it.
i: One number for how wrong this guess was
The model’s probabilities + the right answer
Take the right answer’s probability, compute −ln
Needs only the right answer’s probability: simple and uniform

M5b.t:
At p = 100% the error is 0; as p nears 0 it shoots up (≈ 4.61 at p = 1%).
Confident and wrong is punished hardest, pushing the model to move probability to the right answer.
Averaged over thousands of examples, this is the loss on the training curve.
i: Turns “how good was the guess” into a curve
The logarithm ln with a minus sign
Higher probability, lower error; perfect is 0
Same as maximum likelihood; the gradient is simple

M6a.t:
Training = keep adjusting parameters so the error shrinks. Only one parameter w is drawn: w across, error up.
Real models: this site’s demo has 7406 parameters and large models hundreds of billions, so the error is a valley in very many dimensions; you cannot draw it, but you walk it the same way.
i: Turns training into “find the bottom of the valley”
Parameter w, error L(w)
Change w and the error changes
Makes learning a computable optimisation problem

c: ② The slope shows the way
M6b.t:
Derivative = slope = “move w a tiny bit: how many times that does the error change”. Check: L(0.001) − L(0) ≈ −0.004, ÷0.001 ≈ −4.00.
Negative slope → going right lowers the error; positive → go left. Step against the slope.
With many parameters each has its own slope; the list of them is the “gradient”.
i: Tells each parameter which way to change
The derivative (slope); for many parameters, the gradient
Negative slope → right, positive → left
Only the slope underfoot, yet you get down step by step

M6c.t:
Rule: new w = old w − learning rate × slope (learning rate 0.3).
Near the bottom the slope shrinks, so steps shrink by themselves. Too large a rate (1.1) jumps further and further back and forth; too small (0.05) takes many steps.
i: Moves the parameters step by step to the lowest error
Slope × learning rate = this step
Slope → step → slope again, in a loop
One derivative per step: feasible even for large models

M7a.s: Layer passes to layer, each scaling the change example
M7a.t:
Like a chain of gears: layer 1 ×2, layer 2 ×3, output ×0.5. Move the front a bit: how much does the end move?
That is exactly what training asks: move one parameter a bit, how much does the error change (its derivative).
i: Finds how much the end moves when the front moves
A chain of connected layers
Each layer scales the change up or down
Deep networks are chains of layers; look layer by layer

M7b.s: Total effect = the layers’ factors multiplied example
M7b.t:
This is the chain rule: for functions nested in a chain, the total derivative is the product of each layer’s own derivative.
Why it helps: each layer only needs its own local factor, however complex the whole is. In real networks each factor is a matrix; same idea.
i: Breaks a hard derivative into simple pieces
Each layer’s own local derivative
Multiply the layers’ local derivatives
Each layer minds itself; the whole follows

M7c.s: Back to front, layer by layer (backpropagation) example
M7c.t:
Backpropagation = the chain rule applied once, from output back to input. Every layer’s intermediate results are reused:
one backward pass gives the gradient of every parameter, for roughly one or two times the cost of the forward pass.
The orange arrows in layer 4 ⑤ (send the error back) are this step.
i: Gets every parameter’s gradient in one pass
Results saved going up + each layer’s derivative
Start at the error, multiply layer by layer backwards
Results are reused; nothing recomputed one by one

M8.s: LayerNorm: pull one char’s numbers back to a common range example
M8.t:
Formula: y = (x − μ) ÷ √(σ² + ε), then × γ + β (γ and β are learned; ε is a tiny number to avoid dividing by 0).
E.g. (1.5 − 2.83) ÷ 2.25 ≈ −0.59. However big or small the numbers were, they enter the next block on one scale, so many layers do not drift.
i: Keeps each char’s numbers on one scale
Mean, variance, two learned parameters
Subtract the mean, divide by the std, rescale
Deep stacks do not blow up; training is steadier
